about: The words of the chain house_rival (Data/encounters/chain_house_rival_793.json; Design/content/chains/house_rival.md): the rival Frisian house of Dorestad. Every title, intention, line and label key of its thirteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Thiadbod, Thiadburg, the count (Folcbert), the steward (Hartwin) and the pilot Gerlef are the spine's cast; Meinward, Thiadlef and the lawman are ordinary invented people. One line is quoted: s01.frank_napkins is Notker, De Carolo Magno I.34, in A. J. Grant's translation of 1907 (there the king's own words). The law in the lawman's mouth is the Lex Frisionum, in our own plain rendering. Written 4 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Short cloaks

On the next dam a man of Thiadbod's is selling Frisian cloaks at the old price. Each is a hand shorter than the old length. Thiadbod, the biggest shipman on the river, stands by in a long blue one of his own and watches who buys.
What is the good of those little napkins? I cannot cover myself with them in bed and when I am on horseback I cannot shield myself with them against wind and rain.
You are the one with the Wōkerer's boat. Every summer the dams have a new man. Most are gone by Martinmas.
You are the one with the small boat that is never empty. I have been meaning to come over.
Wool is dear and weavers are slow. A hand off the length, and no one is colder for it but a tall Frank. Sell as I sell and we both eat.
They tell me your tally with the count is closed. A house that owes nothing is a house worth watching.
Cut your own bolts a hand short and match him
Measure the old length aloud, on your own arm, where his buyers can see
Go across and drink his wine
You sell out by noon, and so does he. The Frank buys from neither of you. Nobody on the dams says cheat. They call it keeping up.

You lay a cloak of the old length along your arm and say the spans aloud, twice. A weaver's wife from the back farms laughs and fetches her neighbours. Thiadbod's man stops crying his price while you are at it. Thiadbod goes on smiling.
His wine is good and his news is a week old: wine was dear on the strand at Lundenwic when his ship left it. It may be dear still. He tells you nothing that he learned this morning.
The king's measure

Corn has had the king's price since the synod at Frankfurt, by the king's new measure, in a full year or a hungry one. Thiadbod's man sells rye at that price to the penny. His measure is a finger short. The buyers who came to your boat last time are on his dam.
Oats one penny the measure, barley two, rye three, wheat four. The king's word from Frankfurt. A dozen grains short is short.
Oats two pennies the measure, barley three, rye four, wheat six. The emperor's word from Noviomagus. And gain made by holding corn back he calls filthy.
You are the one who measured cloaks along his arm. Good. Now let us see whose corn is as long as it says.
The king's price, to the penny. Ask anyone. I would not take half a penny over.
You cut cloth. I cut corn. We understand each other.
A measure is a measure. Mine was on this dam before you could walk it.
Ask the steward to try both measures against the king's
Have your own measure marked by the steward and sell heaped, in the open
Say nothing, and take what you carry down to Traiectum

The steward fills Thiadbod's measure from the king's and has corn left in his hand. He counts the grains aloud, by the dozen. Thiadbod is sorry: an old measure, a careless man. He pays the fine before it is asked. The toll man is told to go easy on you for a while.

The measure on Thiadbod's dam today is true to the brim. Someone told him. The steward tries yours twice, to be fair, finds it true, and goes back to his tallies. You have made an old man walk the dams for nothing.

The steward burns his mark into your measure for twelve pennies. You sell by it heaped, where everyone can see, and lose a little on every sack. He orders rye for the count's household from the one measure on the dams that he need not try.
You say nothing. A bishop's town eats too, and at Traiectum nobody stands beside you with a short measure. Rye and barley fetch more there this month.
The dam head

Your place at the dam is taken. Thiadbod has paid the year for the head where you lay, and his big ship is moored across the mouth of the ditch, so that no small boat goes in or out but under her stern. The Maas pilot is his by the year too. He comes down the planks smiling.
The head is paid to Martinmas. A ship must lie somewhere, and she is long.
Your boat is quick and mine is slow. Carry for me this season. You get my word with the toll man, a place at my dam, and thirty pennies in your hand now.
They say you could buy a second boat. Buy into mine. It is safer to be my friend than my neighbour.
And there is your tally with the count. I could buy it from him at Michaelmas. I could also forget which day Michaelmas is.
The steward and I have made it up. He tried my measure and I gave his lord a hawk. You see how things are mended here.
Take his thirty pennies and carry for him this season
Name the law: no man shuts the public way in a river
Lie inside by the ditch and say nothing
You take his silver and his word with the toll man. For a season yours is the quick one of Thiadbod's two boats. Men on the dams stop asking whose she is.

You say it loud enough for three dams to hear: who shuts the public way in a river pays twelve shillings. Thiadbod laughs, and has his ship warped a length upstream before anyone can be sent for. You have your water back. He has stopped smiling at you.
He asks which river. This is a ditch, he says, between his dam and the next, and his dues on it are paid. Nobody on the dam wants to be the one to disagree with him. You lie inside.
You lie inside by the ditch, where loading takes half a day longer. You say nothing. He notices that too.
The cut rope

At first light your boat is not at her post. The rope is cut clean. She lies a bowshot down the river, driven onto the old dam posts, two strakes stove in and the river in her. The man you left to sleep aboard had been called away to drink on Thiadbod's dam.
It was Meinward, with the split ear, that hauls for Thiadbod. He had a knife out at your post. He went down river at cock-crow on a wine boat, for the Maas mouth.
Cut. A rope that parts has a beard on it. This one is shaved. Two strakes and a rib: six days and thirty pennies, or four days of your own hands and the loan of my adze.
If you mean to take it to the court, shout it now. Men remember what they heard before they had eaten.
You carried for him and then you stopped. Men have had worse for less.
You named the law at him before three dams. This is his answer. It came by night because he could not give it by day.
Raise the cry on the dams now, with the cut end in your hand
Go onto Thiadbod's dam with your men and take a pledge
Mend her with your own hands and say nothing yet

You stand on the dam with the cut end in your fist and shout it: your boat, your rope, last night, and the name the boy gave. Men come out of the storehouses. Nobody answers, and everybody has heard. The wright has her on the bank by noon, for thirty pennies.

You go onto his dam with your men behind you and roll two casks of his wine down the planks: a pledge, until he answers. His cellar men stand aside. The Frisian word is pant. The count's court has another word for it. The wright mends her meanwhile, for thirty pennies.

His cellar men are more than yours and they have staves. You come back along the dam with bruises and no wine. All the dams saw you go armed onto another man's ground. The wright mends her meanwhile, for thirty pennies.

You say nothing. Four days on the bank with the wright's adze and your own hands, and she swims again. The wright says less than he knows. He does say that a wine boat takes two days to the Maas mouth, and that Meinward cannot swim.
The man with the split ear

Witla, the strand at the Maas mouth: boats in the creek, nets drying, a pilot's shed on the bank. This is where the wine boat brought Meinward. The pilot here is old Gerlef, and Thiadbod pays him by the year.
Split ear? He sleeps in my net shed and eats Thiadbod's bread. I was told to keep him here and on no account let him over the water. Odd, for a man they want rid of.
He went out on the ebb with an English boat, days since. Over the water. No Frisian court will hear him now.
The one with the split ear? Gone over the water long since, and the court has sat, they tell me. Then it no longer matters where he went.
I am paid to pilot. I am not paid to lie. I am forty, and I have seen that bar move nine times in fifty years.
I cut a rope. I did not ask whose. Six pennies and bread, and stay in the land, he said. While I am in the land nothing can be asked of him. I do not know what he meant.
Take him, and bring him up the river to the court
Hear him before the pilot and two fishermen, then give him six pennies to go over the water
Leave the man be, and ask the pilot about the bar
He runs for the flats and your men have him before the tide does. He comes up the river in the bottom of your boat, tied, saying nothing. Gerlef watches you go and does not lift a hand.
He is faster over mud than any of you. A fishing boat takes him off the flats and stands out past the bar on the ebb. One of your men has turned his knee. Meinward has left the land.

He says it before Gerlef and two men mending nets: who paid him, how much, and which post. Fishermen forget nothing that costs them nothing. Then he goes aboard an English boat with your pennies in his fist. He has left the land.
You let the man lie. Gerlef talks to the water for a while and then, since you asked, to you: she runs north of the bank since the winter floods, and the old mark on the dune is no use now.
The count's court

The count's court sits under the open sky by Saint Martin's church. Seven sworn men find the judgment and an old Frisian says the law. Your matter is called: a boat cut from her post by night. Thiadbod stands across the ring with five free men behind him.
The king's court. Shipman, say your say and be short. I have a hawk waiting.
The emperor's court. Shipman, say your say and be short. I have a hawk waiting.
I know this shipman, and I think well of him. That is not law, and I do not pretend that it is.
You again. The king's man heard you once. Here you are heard by me.
On other days you sit with the seven. Today another man has your stool, and you stand where the wronged man stands.
Our law is not written. It is in my head, where no mouse has got at it.
They wrote our law down at Aachen, from what men like me told them. They got most of it.
Who takes a man's thing pays it twice, and his own man-price to the king for the peace. Who denies it clears himself with five free men, his own hand the sixth.

Who sets another on: if the doer has fled the land, the setter pays a third or swears. If the doer stands in the land, the setter neither swears nor pays. He bears the wronged man's enmity until he wins his friendship back.
A pledge taken by force we call pant. What spoils while the taker holds it, the taker pays.
I was at Mass. Half the dams saw me. Ropes part, rivers run. I am sorry for his boat, and I said so before he asked.
Bring Meinward into the ring
Charge Thiadbod as the setter-on, with your witnesses; let him swear if he can
Charge him on your own word alone
Take the sixty pennies he offers in the porch and let it drop

Meinward is shown the kettle: a stone to be taken out of boiling water, the hand bound and sealed three nights. He looks at it and tells everything. He owes you your boat twice over and owns a knife and six pennies; the count takes him to work it off on the dams. Then the old man turns to Thiadbod. The doer stands in the land: the setter neither swears nor pays. He bears your enmity, lawfully, until he wins your friendship back. And the old man adds a judgment of his own: a boat at her post is a house on the water, and who looses her by night pays as for a house burned. No one had said that before.

Thiadbod's five come forward to the relics. The fourth stops. He heard what was said about that night, he says, and he has a boat of his own. An oath of five is not an oath of six. Thiadbod pays the setter's third on the spot, two hundred pennies, as if it were a small thing.

Five free men lay their hands on the relics after him, one by one. The oath is whole. By the law he is clean, and you have named a clean man before the court. People look at who stood behind him, and remember.

You have no one behind you. You say it anyway, plainly, and look at each of his five in turn. The youngest will not come to the relics. An oath of five is not an oath of six. Thiadbod pays the setter's third, two hundred pennies, and does not look at the boy.
Your word against six hands. The law is not in doubt, and the seven do not take long. He is clean. The count asks whether you have anything else, since his hawk has waited.
In the church porch, before the court sits, he puts sixty pennies in your hand for the wright. He is sorry for your boat. Your matter is called, and you say you have none.
Thiadburg's storehouse
Thiadburg sends for you. She keeps the storehouse on the dam that her husband built, lends on goods, and is Thiadbod's elder sister. She does not trust him with her keys.
The law says he bears your enmity until he wins your friendship back. He sent me to ask what it costs. I came to see who was asking.
He paid the third and smiled. He has not smiled since. He sent me to ask if that is the end of it.
He swore with five. Two of them owe me silver, so I know what their hands are worth. He sent me to see whether you will be quiet now.
You took his sixty pennies in the porch. He thinks he knows your price. I am not sure that he does.
And his two casks. He counts them twice a day. Keep them or send them back, but he has not stopped counting.
You mended your boat with your own hands and said nothing for forty nights. He does not know what to make of that. Nor do I, yet.
I ask what a thing weighs before I ask what it cost. What does this weigh with you?
Name a price in silver, and take it
Name the price of the friendship the law left open
Ask nothing of him. Ask her for room under her roof
Tell her it stands as it stands
You name a sum. She halves it, you halve the difference, and she counts out a hundred and twenty pennies herself. 'Now he thinks it is over,' she says. 'So do you, perhaps.'
You name a sum fit for a man's friendship. She does not blink. She counts out a pound of silver, two hundred and forty pennies, and says he will call it cheap by Easter.

'Room under my roof, and nothing from him?' She is a little amused. She gives you a place at the dry end, and an order for cloth to go with it. A brother who cannot be trusted with her keys has bought her a new neighbour.
'Then it stands,' she says. 'I will tell him you said it without shouting. That will worry him more.'
A ship on the bank

A big merchant ship lies on a bank where the channel ran last year, heeled over, with casks in the water round her. Men stand on her high side. She is Thiadbod's. The flood is making, and the bank will be under before the tide is half up.
This is the year the storms broke so many ships in the English sea.
The bank was not here at Easter. Ask the pilot. Ask anyone.
I will not ask it of you. You can see what there is to see.
You said yourself that it stands as it stands. I am only telling you how many we are.
We are nine. I can swim. The others cannot.
Take the men off and leave the wine
Take the men off, and four casks for your trouble
Lay out his anchor and try to float her on the flood
Stand off. There are fishing boats; let them earn it

Nine men in a boat built for four. You leave the wine to the flood. One cask has burst on the bank, and it is not wine in the straw: sword blades, greased, bound for the north. Thiadbod sees you see them. He sits in the bottom boards beside his son and says nothing all the way in.

The men come aboard, and four casks after them, over her high side. 'For your trouble,' he says, before you can say it. A fifth cask has burst on the bank, and it is not wine in the straw: sword blades, greased, bound for the north. He sees you see them.

Your steersman lays Thiadbod's anchor out in the deep water from your boat, and his men heave as the flood lifts her. She comes off groaning and swims, leaking, with half her wine. One burst cask is left on the bank, and it is not wine in the straw: sword blades. He pays your men on the spot, with both hands, and does not look back at it.

She lifts, turns, and breaks her back on the edge of the bank. You take the men off with the water at their belts; one of yours is hurt at the rope. The casks go out on the ebb, all but one that bursts on the sand: sword blades in straw. He sees you see them.
You stand off and watch. A fishing boat takes them off at the last of it. The ship stays. Your crew do not talk much that evening. The ones who pray, pray.
The reckoning

Word of the bank reached Dorestat before you did. Thiadbod's wine was bought on trust up the river, and the men he owes have come down to the dams. He and his sister are waiting for you. What the two houses are to each other from now on is settled today.
You took me off the bank. I had your rope cut. Both are true, and I have to stand here and hold both.
You floated her. I would not have floated yours. I have thought about that every night since.
You stood off and watched. I would have done the same. I do not forgive it either.
You saw what was in the straw. You have not said. I count that too.
You took silver for your friendship at my sister's hands. I do not ask for it back. I ask what it bought.
He has a dam head and a name. You have a small boat that is never empty. Put them together or pull them apart, but do it before the count's steward does it for you.
Your cloth is dry under my roof. I say it so that you know I am not only his sister.
Offer him fellowship: two boats, one reckoning
Let the law and his losses run, and be at the steward's sale
Say before witnesses that there is no peace between the houses
He is silent a long while. Then: 'At the next court, in the church porch. Forty nights. I will bring what I have left.'
You say you will be at the steward's sale. Thiadbod nods as a man nods at a price. His son looks at you until his father turns him by the shoulder.
You say it before his sister and the men from up the river: no peace. 'Then say it where it counts,' he says, 'at the court, in forty nights.' He sounds almost glad to know.
Two boats, one reckoning

The porch of Saint Martin's church, forty nights on. Two houses will bear each other's fire and wreck and count the gain of two boats together. The king's law lets men make such agreements, for alms, for fire and for shipwreck. It forbids them to swear to it. Thiadbod wants the oath.
You may agree. You may not swear to it; the king has said so since Herstal. I would rather not hear an oath that I must then say I did not hear.
An agreement without an oath is a rope without a knot. But I have been wrong about ropes.
Half of what she carries is yours while she swims. I have said it before witnesses. Now say yours.
And there will be no more iron in the straw. That was my trade, not ours.
Where I come from we say man is man's delight. We also count the silver twice.
Make it before witnesses, without the oath, as the king allows
Swear it on the altar, each to the other
Make it without the oath, and open the chest to every boat on the dams

Hands, witnesses, a tally split down the middle. From today Thiadbod's boat sails with yours, and the gain and loss of both are counted together. Your share of the first reckoning is seven hundred pennies. The Dane who watched from the dam gives you a stick with a verse cut on it, for luck.

You swear it on the altar, when the priest has found something to do in the churchyard. A sworn band is stronger, and it is forbidden: the count will hear of it by evening and keep it by him, as he keeps everything. Your share of the first reckoning is nine hundred pennies. The Dane who watched gives you a stick with a verse cut on it.

You make it without the oath, and say that any boat on the dams may come in on the same terms: a penny in the chest for each voyage, and the chest pays for fire, for wreck and for the poor at the church door. By Martinmas eleven boats are in. Thiadbod gives what he would give a brother: the Maas marks out of old Gerlef's head, taught to your steersman, and the first reckoning, fourteen hundred pennies. The Dane who watched gives you a stick with a verse cut on it. No one has done this at Dorestat before.
The steward's sale

Forty nights on, the count's steward sells what Thiadbod has to pay what Thiadbod owes: the dam head with its storehouse posts, the last of his wine, and what is left of his name. Thiadbod stands at the back with his son. He is going up the Rhine to the Frisians' shore at Mogontia, to carry other men's wine.
A dam head, six rods by forty. Storehouse posts, sound. Eleven casks: a dozen, less one. Who speaks?
Your claim stands first, by the court's finding. The rest take what is left.
The king's men have asked what a wine ship wanted with iron in her casks. That is not on my tally. I only sell what is left.
Speak up. It is a good dam. I chose it myself.
The hull is still on the bank. The sea did not want her either.
Take the dam head as your price
Take the hull off the bank and have her mended
Let his sister have the dam head, and keep your place under her roof
Take the dam head, and leave him a boat and your wine to carry at Mogontia

The dam head is yours: a place of your own at Dorestat, with three casks and four hundred and fifty pennies over when his debts are met. Thiadbod goes up the river on another man's barge. His son looks back once. He is fourteen, and he has a good memory.

You have her floated off on a spring tide and towed to the wright: a sea-going ship, yours for the mending, and six hundred pennies from the sale besides. Thiadbod watches her come up the river past his old dam. His son watches you.

You speak for Thiadburg, and no one bids against the two of you. She has the dam head she always said was hers. You have the dry end of her storehouse for as long as it stands, a woman there who knows what everything weighs, and seven hundred pennies from the sale. Thiadbod goes up the river. 'She will rob you fairly,' he says.

You take the dam head, and leave him the old wine boat and a third of what he carries for you. He looks at you a long time. 'I would not have done that either,' he says. On the Frisians' shore at Mogontia there is now a man who buys your wine at the press and owes you his bread. Your share of the sale is eleven hundred pennies.
No peace

The court again, forty nights on. You say it before the count and the seven: there is no peace between your house and Thiadbod's. The old Frisian says what the law leaves even to a man at feud. The bishop's clerk from Traiectum is listening too.

A man at feud has peace in church, in his own house, on the way to church and back, on the way to court and back. Who kills him there pays nine times thirty shillings. Everywhere else he looks to himself.
The king wants his shipmen alive and paying toll. Do it on the water, where I need not hear of it.
The emperor's word is that the wronged shall take the price and make a lasting peace. You will hear that again from men less patient than I am.
The emperor's word from Thionville is that feuds are settled, and the stubborn are sent to him. Do not make me send you.
Saint Martin's men on these banks answer to Saint Martin. The count lodges no one on them and takes nothing of theirs. A pound of wax at Martinmas is not much to pay.
This one is Saint Martin's already. Whoever touches him touches the saint. I say it so that it has been said.
I hear him. Let it be remembered, since no one here can write but the clerk.
At home we have a verse about a foe's friends. It is short. Most of ours are.
Put your house and your boats under Saint Martin's hand
Float his hull off the bank and keep her, by the strong hand
Stand alone: arm the crew and hang the cut rope over your door

You give yourself and your boats to Saint Martin at Traiectum: wax every Martinmas, and the bishop's hand over your door. The count cannot lodge men on you or seize your goods, and Thiadbod will not touch what is the saint's. What you took of his on the river this season, seven hundred pennies' worth, you keep. The bishop is pleased. The count is not. Thiadbod's son learns your face. The Dane in the ring gives you a stick with a verse cut on it.

You float his ship off the bank with armed men standing on the sand, and bring her up the river as your own. By the custom of the strand she is wreck. By Thiadbod's reckoning she is stolen, and his sons will reckon it so after him. What you took of his on the river this season sells for six hundred pennies. The Dane in the ring gives you a stick with a verse cut on it.

You hang the cut rope over your own door. Your crew go armed on the dams. What you take of Thiadbod's wine on the river that season sells for a thousand pennies. Nobody undersells you now. Nobody stands very near you either. The Dane in the ring gives you a stick with a verse cut on it.
At the church door

Thiadbod lies in the ground by Saint Martin's, and so does the one who said there was no peace. His heir has the house now, and the feud with it, as you have yours. You meet at the church door, where the law gives even the two of you peace.
They say my house cut your house's rope. Yours always said so. Mine never said that it did not.
I have carried this since I was fourteen. It is heavier than wine and it pays nothing.
The heathen men burn us both alike. They do not ask which house.
You are the saint's and I am the count's. Those two do not love each other either.
In here you have peace, both of you. I would be glad if some of it went out of the door with you.
End it: a marriage between the houses, and the old price paid
Pledge faith and take his price, as the emperor's law orders
Keep it. The rope stays over the door

You pay for the wine and the hull, he pays for the rope, and the two sums cross on the church step and nearly cancel: it costs you a pound of silver. The rest is a marriage between the houses, agreed in the porch, with his dam and yours behind it. The cut rope is burned under the bride-ale. His boat sails with yours from that day.
He counts three hundred pennies into your hand before the priest: the rope, the boat, the years. You pledge faith. It is a lasting peace by the emperor's law, and a thin one by any other.
'Then keep it,' he says. 'I will keep mine.' You go into the church by the same door, one after the other, and stand on opposite sides.

This year, at the count's court at Dorestat, a hired man owned to cutting a boat from her post by night. Thiadbod the shipman, named as the setter-on, neither swore nor paid, as the Frisians' law has it, and bears the enmity of the house he wronged.
This year, at the count's court at Dorestat, Thiadbod the shipman could not find his five for the oath, and paid the setter's third for a boat cut from her post.
This year, at the count's court at Dorestat, Thiadbod the shipman swore himself clean with five free men of a charge about a cut rope.
This year two houses of Dorestat that had been at law made one reckoning of their two boats, against fire and wreck.
This year the shipmen of Dorestat made a common chest against fire and wreck, a penny for each voyage, without an oath, as the king's law allows.
This year Thiadbod's dam head at Dorestat was sold by the count's steward for his debts, and he went up the Rhine to Mogontia.
This year it was said before the count's court at Dorestat that there is no peace between two houses of shipmen there.
This year the heirs of two houses of Dorestat, long at feud over a cut rope, made a lasting peace at the church door.

A dam at Dorestat on a bright, windy morning: a seller holds up a blue cloak that ends at his knee; a tall Frank in a red cloak measures it against himself with scorn; behind them Thiadbod, well fed, in a long blue cloak with a silver pin, watches the player's small boat.

Midday on the dam under a grey sky: the thin old steward pours grain from one wooden measure into another over a cloth and counts on his fingers; Thiadbod stands by with open hands; sacks and a line of farm wives behind.

Evening, low sun on the water: a big merchant ship, twice the length of the player's boat, moored across the mouth of a ditch between two earth dams, shutting in a small boat; Thiadbod comes down a plank smiling, a purse held out in one hand.

First light, mist on the river: a small clinker boat driven onto old black posts, half full of water; in front a hand holds the clean-cut end of a rope; a boy points down the river; a shipwright with an adze looks on.

Low tide at the Maas mouth, wide flats under a pale grey sky: an old pilot with a sounding pole taller than himself stands at the door of a net shed; inside, a young man with a split ear sits on a heap of nets.

Open ground beside a small timber church at noon, a dry wind: a ring of men; the count seated with a sword across his knees; an old Frisian speaking with one hand raised; Thiadbod with five men behind him; an iron kettle steaming over a fire at the edge of the ring.
Inside a storehouse on a dam, afternoon light through the gaps in the planks: bales and casks; Thiadburg, upright, in a white head-cloth with keys at her belt, weighs silver on a small folding scale.

A big merchant ship with one mast, heeled over on a sandbank in a rising grey sea, wind from the west, late afternoon: casks afloat; nine men on her high side, a boy among them; one burst cask on the sand showing straw and iron; the player's small boat coming up under oars.
The dam head at Dorestat in flat late-afternoon light: Thiadbod bareheaded, his rings gone, his sister beside him; behind them strangers from up the river sit on his casks and wait.

The porch of the timber church on a clear cold morning: two men clasp hands over a split tally stick; a priest looks away toward the graveyard; a Dane leans on the fence, watching; below, two boats lie side by side.

The dam head on a grey morning in light rain: the steward stands on a cask with a bundle of notched sticks; bidders in a half ring; at the back Thiadbod and his son with a bundle each, and a river barge waiting.

The court ring by the church under a hard bright sky: two groups of men stand apart; the count on his feet, pointing; between them the old Frisian with both hands raised; a clerk with a wax tablet at the side.

The church door on a still autumn morning, a generation later: two people of middle years face each other on the step, neither armed, a priest in the doorway behind; over a house door in the distance hangs an old grey rope.
